name: Blood Pressure Monitor with Blood Pressure Cuff (Medical Diagnostic Pack, Blue)
stowage: Medical Diagnostic Pack (Blue): monitor at B4, large and small cuffs at B2 (2015 list)
steps: Take the Blood Pressure Monitor and a cuff out of the blue Medical Diagnostic Pack.
Pick the cuff size that fits the arm (large or small).
Connect the cuff to the monitor.
Roll up the sleeve so the arm is bare.
Wrap the cuff around the upper arm. Line it up with the marks printed on the cuff.
Make sure the person is held in place (strap or foot loops) so they do not drift.
Press the On/Off button. The cuff fills and measures by itself.
Read the pulse and the blood pressure on the screen.
Write down both numbers and the time.
microgravityNotes: No microgravity change to the cuff method was found in the public procedure. Expect lower readings in flight: one ISS study found 24 h average systolic pressure about 8 mmHg lower than before flight (Norsk 2015). The 2001 checklist takes vital signs with the patient restrained.
failureModes: No reading or error: the device-level fix is in procedure 2.0.304, which is NOT FOUND in public sources. Use manual pulse count (eq-manual-pulse) and tell the ground.
Cuff wrong size: change to the other cuff (large or small) and repeat.

name: Automatic Blood Pressure Cuff (ABPC), Advanced Life Support Pack
stowage: Advanced Life Support Pack (ALSP), item ALSP-4 (2001 checklist; listed in ALSP contents in 2011 catalog)
steps: Take the automatic cuff (ABPC) out of the Advanced Life Support Pack.
Plug the cuff hose into the device.
Bare the upper arm.
Wrap the cuff on the arm with the rubber tube on the inside of the arm.
Put the lower edge of the cuff about 2.5 cm (one inch) above the elbow crease.
Press POWER. Wait until the screen shows 0.
Press START. The cuff fills by itself and then measures.
Wait for the beep. The top and bottom blood pressure numbers appear.
Watch the screen. It switches between blood pressure and pulse every 2 seconds.
Write down blood pressure and pulse now. The memory keeps blood pressure only, not pulse.
Press POWER to switch off. Unplug the hose before you pack it away.
microgravityNotes: NOT FOUND: the 2001 procedure gives no microgravity-specific cuff step. Other procedures in the same checklist take vital signs with the patient restrained.
failureModes: No reading: press SELECT to choose the next higher inflation setting, then press START again.
Pulse lost: pulse is not saved in memory, so repeat the measurement if you missed it.

name: Blood Oximeter (pulse oximeter), Medical Diagnostic Pack (Blue)

steps: Take the Blood Oximeter out of the blue Medical Diagnostic Pack.
Put four AA batteries in it.
Plug the finger sensor into the oximeter.
Put the sensor on a finger.
Press the Power button.
Press the Display button until a red dot sits over SpO2 in the top window.
Read the SpO2 number and write it down with the time.
Press and hold Power to switch off.
When the doctor says you are done, take the batteries out and pack it away.

name: Manual pulse and breathing count (fingers and a clock, no device)
stowage: No hardware. Needs a watch or timer.
steps: Find the pulse on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb, with two fingers.
Count the beats for 15 seconds.
Multiply that number by 4. This is the heart rate per minute.
Watch the chest rise for 15 seconds and count the breaths.
Multiply by 4. This is the breathing rate per minute.
Write both numbers down with the time.
If a number is not normal or keeps changing, check again about every 5 minutes.
microgravityNotes: No change to the counting method was found. One ISS study found resting heart rate in long flight was unchanged from the ground (Norsk 2015). Pulse sites listed in the 2001 checklist are radial (wrist) and pedal (foot).
failureModes: Cannot feel the pulse at the wrist: try the foot (pedal pulse), which the 2001 checklist also lists.
No pulse and no breathing: this is an emergency. Start CPR per the medical checklist.

name: Oral Disposable Thermometer (Tempa-DOT dot-matrix strip)
stowage: 2001: Ambulatory Medical Pack P3-A2 and ALSP Assessment-4. 2015: 'Thermometer' in Medical Diagnostic Pack (Blue) at B3, type not stated.
steps: Do not eat or drink for 15 minutes before.
Open one thermometer strip.
Put it under the tongue, as far back as it goes. The dots can face up or down.
Press the tongue down on it and keep the mouth closed for 60 seconds.
Take it out and wait about 10 seconds.
Find the last blue dot. That is the temperature. Skip any dot that did not turn blue in the middle.
Write down the temperature and the time.
Throw the strip away. It is single use.
If it is above 37.8 °C, contact the flight surgeon.
microgravityNotes: No change to the oral method was found. Expect a higher baseline: a peer-reviewed ISS study found resting core body temperature rose about 1 °C over 2.5 months in flight (Stahn 2017). Use the crew member's in-flight baseline, not the Earth value, when judging fever (team inference; needs surgeon review).
failureModes: Left in mouth too long: the maker says retake with a new strip.
Dots already blue before use: the strip was stored too warm. The maker says dots turn blue above 35 °C in storage. Use another strip.
Below 35.5 °C or above 40.4 °C: the strip cannot read it. Report 'off scale' and tell the ground.
Steps are from the commercial maker's instructions (grade C). The ISS-specific how-to-use page was NOT FOUND.

name: Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer (PCBA, i-STAT) with EC6+ cartridge and Fingerstix
unit: mg/dL (also Na, K, iCa mmol/L, pH, Hct %, Hb g/dL)
stowage: Ambulatory Medical Pack (AMP), Blood Analyzer Pack (2001 and 2011)
steps: Tape a strip of gray tape near you to hold small items so they do not float away.
Get out gloves, a cleaning wipe, gauze, a bandage, one EC6+ cartridge, a capillary tube, the capillary bulb, and a Fingerstix lancet.
Open the cartridge packet but leave the cartridge inside for now.
Put on gloves.
Warm the finger.
Clean the fingertip with the wipe. Let it dry.
Press the Fingerstix hard on the fingertip to prick it. Put the used lancet in the zip bag.
Squeeze the finger gently. Wipe away the first drop with gauze.
Squeeze gently again. Touch the end of the capillary tube to the drop.
Fill the tube two thirds to three quarters full. Check there are no bubbles.
Press gauze on the finger until bleeding stops. Put on a bandage.
Hold the cartridge by its sides only. Fix the bulb to the tube.
Cover the bulb hole with a finger and squeeze gently. Fill the cartridge to the fill mark. Do not overfill.
If bubbles are stuck, tap the cartridge. If they stay, throw it away and start again with a new one.
Snap the cartridge lid shut.
Push the cartridge into the analyzer door as far as it goes. Do not pull it out while LCK shows.
Type an operator number and a patient number when asked. Press ENT each time.
Wait 120 seconds for results.
Write down the Glu number (glucose, mg/dL) and the other results.
Remove the cartridge. Put all waste in the zip bag, then in biohazard trash.
microgravityNotes: The checklist adds steps for floating items: tape small items down near the work area. A shuttle study found the analyzer reliable in flight, and in-flight changes were likely due to how the blood sample was collected (Smith 1997). Cartridges are reported to have a 6 month shelf life, which limits use (secondary source, see evidence gap).
failureModes: INSUFFICIENT SAMPLE: repeat the sample with a new cartridge (steps 2 to 21 of the checklist).
Bubbles stay in the cartridge: discard it and fill another one.
LCK stays on the screen: do not pull the cartridge out. Contact the surgeon.
Battery error: battery change procedure is in a separate HMS malfunction section, NOT FOUND in public sources.
No cartridges in date: no glucose reading is possible with this device. Report it. Urine strip glucose (eq-urine-chemstrip) is a rough backup only.

name: Urine Chemstrip (CHEMSTRIP 10SG) with Color Chart
unit: color-chart categories (SpG, pH, leukocytes, nitrite, protein, glucose, ketones, urobilinogen, bilirubin, blood)
stowage: 2015: Topical & Injectable Medication Pack (Brown), B3. 2001: AMP P4-A3.
steps: Put on gloves.
Hold two cotton swabs together under the urine stream until they are soaked.
Wipe the two swabs over the colored pads on the strip.
Wait the time printed for the strip.
Hold the strip next to the color chart and match each pad.
Write down each result.
Put the swabs and strip in biohazard trash.
microgravityNotes: Microgravity change: urine is collected on cotton swabs held in the stream, not in a cup, then wiped on the strip.
failureModes: Wait time for reading: 'recommended time' is not stated in the public checklist (NOT FOUND).

name: Eye Chart (Visual Acuity Card, near vision)
unit: letters correct / letters on line, per eye
stowage: 2015: Medical Diagnostic Pack (Blue), stowed with Locator Card. 2001/2011: AMP Physical Exam Pack (Physical Exam-1).
steps: Take the eye chart (visual acuity card) out of the medical kit.
Hold the card about 40 cm from the person's eyes, or have a helper hold it.
Cover one eye with a hand.
Read the lowest line you can.
Write down how many letters you got right out of how many letters are on that line.
Cover the other eye and do the same again.
Write down which eye each result is for.
microgravityNotes: NOT FOUND: no source describes a microgravity change. The card floats, so it must be held or fixed at about 40 cm (team inference, not sourced).
failureModes: Cannot read any line: write 'unable to read top line' for that eye and tell the ground.
Card not found: the 2015 list stows it with the Locator Card. No backup method was found in the sources.

name: Space Station Eyewash (SSE) with eyewash goggles (Crew Contamination Protection Kit)
stowage: 2011: Eyewash Kit launched on the CCPK, then velcroed on panel SM-329 near the SVO-ZV water port in the Russian Service Module.
steps: Take out contact lenses if the person wears them.
Flush the eye right away with water from a drink bag and straw. Use towels to soak up water.
Set up the eyewash next to the water port (SVO-ZV).
Connect the supply hose to the water port and the waste hose to an empty wastewater bag.
Put on the goggles with the outflow side on the hurt eye.
Pump the water port about four times.
Press the goggles against the face for a better seal.
Push and hold the red release valve to start water into the goggles.
Keep the eyes open while the water flows.
Keep pumping as needed. Soak up leaks with towels.
When the bag is full, let go of the valve and change to an empty bag.
Keep flushing until the pain goes away or the surgeon says stop.
Contact the surgeon.
microgravityNotes: Designed for microgravity: water goes into sealed goggles and out to a wastewater bag so it does not float free. A drink bag and straw are used first. The 2001 procedure also has an optional numbing eye drop step (proparacaine) that needs surgeon direction; it is not included in these plain steps.
failureModes: Hoses come loose from the goggle lenses: a known ground-unit issue, fixed with hose clamps per the 2011 catalog.
Eyewash not set up yet: keep flushing with the drink bag and straw.
The 2015 manual names a different port (CBO-3B) and procedure 2.3.304, which is NOT FOUND in public sources. Check which port your vehicle uses.
